name: Schwarzschild Radius
description: The boundary radius (event horizon) at which a body of mass m becomes a black hole. If all of the mass is compressed within this radius, not even light can escape. It is about 3 km for the Sun's mass and about 9 mm for the Earth's.
notes: g is the gravitational constant (6.674e-11) and c is the speed of light. This assumes a non-rotating, uncharged (Schwarzschild) black hole; a rotating body needs the more complex Kerr solution.

name: Circular Orbital Velocity
description: Gives the speed needed for a circular orbit as sqrt(G·M/r), where M is the central mass and r the orbital radius. It is the velocity at which gravity exactly provides the centripetal force.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m) so the speed comes out in m/s; r is measured from the center of the central body, not its surface. It assumes M is much larger than the orbiting mass.

name: Kepler's Third Law (Orbital Period)
description: Computes the orbital period from Kepler's third law as 2·pi·sqrt(a^3/(G·M)), with a the semi-major axis and M the central mass. It gives how long one full orbit takes.
notes: Use SI units (m, kg) to get the period in seconds; the result is the time for one complete orbit. It assumes the central mass dominates the orbiting body's mass.

name: Surface Gravity
description: Calculates the gravitational acceleration at a body's surface as G·M/r^2, with M the mass and r the radius. It is the acceleration a freely falling object experiences at that surface.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m) for acceleration in m/s^2; r is the body's radius from its center. This assumes a spherical, uniform body and ignores rotation.

name: Stefan-Boltzmann Luminosity
description: Computes the total power radiated by a spherical blackbody as 4·pi·r^2·sigma·T^4, combining surface area with the Stefan-Boltzmann law. Luminosity rises with the square of radius and the fourth power of temperature.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin and radius in meters for the result in watts. It assumes an ideal blackbody; real stars need an emissivity factor below 1.

name: Apparent Brightness (Flux)
description: Gives the observed flux from a source as its luminosity divided by the area of a sphere of radius d, L/(4·pi·d^2). It shows how brightness falls off with the square of distance.
notes: Use SI units (W, m) for flux in W/m^2; d is the distance from source to observer. It assumes the source radiates uniformly and ignores absorption along the path.

name: Distance Modulus
description: Computes the distance modulus 5·log10(d) - 5 for a distance in parsecs. It is the difference between apparent and absolute magnitude that encodes how far away a star is.
notes: Distance must be in parsecs; the formula is defined so the modulus is zero at 10 pc. It assumes no interstellar extinction, which would otherwise add to the value.

name: Stellar Parallax Distance
description: Finds the distance to a star as the reciprocal of its parallax angle, giving distance in parsecs from a parallax in arcseconds. A parsec is defined as the distance yielding a parallax of one arcsecond.
notes: The parallax must be in arcseconds for the result in parsecs. Small measurement errors matter greatly for distant stars, where the parallax angle is tiny.

name: Redshift Recession Velocity
description: Estimates a galaxy's recession velocity as the redshift z multiplied by the speed of light, v = z·c. It converts an observed spectral redshift into a receding speed.
notes: This linear approximation holds only for small redshifts (z much less than 1); at high z a relativistic or cosmological treatment is required. Redshift is dimensionless.

name: Hubble's Law
description: Applies Hubble's law v = H·d to give a galaxy's recession velocity from its distance and the Hubble constant. It expresses the uniform expansion of the universe.
notes: Units must be consistent: with H in km/s/Mpc and d in Mpc, velocity is in km/s. The relation is an approximation best suited to relatively nearby galaxies.

name: Angular Size
description: Computes the angular size an object subtends as 2·atan(s/(2·d)), from its physical size s and distance d. It gives the full angle in radians the object spans in the sky.
notes: Physical size and distance must share the same length unit; the result is in radians. For far-away objects the angle is very small and nearly equals s/d.

name: Magnitude Difference
description: Calculates the magnitude difference between two sources as -2.5·log10(f1/f2) from their fluxes. It converts a brightness ratio into the astronomical magnitude scale.
notes: Both fluxes need the same unit. A brighter source (larger flux) gives a smaller, more negative magnitude, following the inverted magnitude convention.

name: Light Travel Time
description: Computes how long light takes to cross a distance as the distance divided by the speed of light, d/c. It gives the time delay for light or any signal traveling at light speed.
notes: Use consistent units (meters and m/s give seconds). This is the travel time in a vacuum; a medium would slow light and increase the time.

name: Mean Planetary Density
description: Calculates a planet's mean density by dividing its mass by the volume of a sphere, m/((4/3)·pi·r^3). It gives the average density assuming the body is a uniform sphere.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m) for density in kg/m^3; r is the planet's radius. This is a mean value and does not capture the denser core or lighter outer layers.

name: Wien's Displacement Law
description: Gives the wavelength at which a blackbody at temperature t emits most strongly, as the Wien constant b divided by the temperature. Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths, which is why hot stars look blue and cooler ones red.
notes: Temperature must be an absolute temperature in kelvin. The Wien constant b ≈ 2.898×10⁻³ m·K applies to the wavelength form; a different constant is used for the frequency form.

name: Roche Limit (Rigid)
description: Estimates the minimum orbital distance at which a rigid satellite can hold together against tidal forces, as the primary's radius times the cube root of twice the density ratio. Inside this distance tidal forces would tear the satellite apart.
notes: This is the rigid-body approximation; fluid bodies have a larger Roche limit (about 2.44 r for equal densities). Distance is measured from the primary's center, and both densities must use the same units.

name: Relativistic Doppler Shift (Receding)
description: Computes the observed frequency of light from a source moving directly away, as the source frequency times sqrt((1 − v/c)/(1 + v/c)). A receding source is shifted to lower frequency (redshifted), following special relativity.
notes: This form applies to a source receding along the line of sight; use v as a positive recession speed below c. For an approaching source the sign of v is reversed.

name: Angular Resolution (Rayleigh)
description: Gives the smallest angular separation a circular aperture can resolve by the Rayleigh criterion, as 1.22 times the wavelength divided by the aperture diameter. Larger apertures and shorter wavelengths give finer resolution.
notes: Result is in radians and assumes a circular aperture limited only by diffraction. Wavelength and diameter must share length units; atmospheric seeing often dominates real telescopes.

name: Blackbody Flux (Stefan-Boltzmann)
description: Computes the total power radiated per unit surface area by an ideal blackbody as the Stefan-Boltzmann constant times temperature to the fourth power. Doubling the temperature increases the emitted flux sixteenfold.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin). This is the flux for a perfect emitter; a real surface's output is scaled by its emissivity between 0 and 1.

name: Gravitational Binding Energy
description: Gives the gravitational binding energy of a uniform-density sphere, 3GM²/(5R), which is the energy needed to disperse its mass to infinity. Larger, more massive, denser bodies are bound more tightly.
notes: Assumes a sphere of uniform density; real bodies with centrally concentrated mass are bound more tightly. The result is a positive magnitude, though binding energy is often quoted as negative.

name: Tidal Force
description: Estimates the differential tidal force stretching a satellite of mass mm across its radius, from a primary of mass m at orbital distance r. The force grows sharply as the orbit shrinks, scaling as 1/r³.
notes: This is the difference in gravitational pull across the body, not the total attraction; it falls off as the cube of distance. It assumes a point-mass primary and the satellite radius small compared to the orbit.

name: Roche Limit
description: Computes the Roche limit, the orbital distance inside which a fluid satellite is torn apart by tidal forces, from the primary radius and the two densities. It scales with the cube root of the density ratio.
notes: Uses the coefficient 2.44 for a fluid, self-gravitating body; a more rigid satellite survives closer in. Densities, not masses, drive the result, and the distance is measured from the primary's center.

name: Telescope Angular Resolution
description: Gives the diffraction-limited angular resolution of a telescope in radians, 1.22 times the wavelength divided by the aperture diameter. Smaller values mean finer detail can be separated.
notes: This is the theoretical Rayleigh limit; atmospheric seeing and optical flaws usually make real resolution worse. Wavelength and aperture must share units so the ratio is dimensionless.

name: Small-Angle (Physical Size)
description: Uses the small-angle approximation, size equals distance times angular size, to find the true physical size of a distant object. It works when the angle is small and given in radians.
notes: The angle must be in radians and small (well under one radian) for the linear approximation to hold. Distance and result share the same length unit.

name: Stellar Luminosity
description: Applies the Stefan-Boltzmann law to a sphere, 4πR²σT⁴, giving the total radiant power emitted by a star from its radius and surface temperature. Luminosity rises with the fourth power of temperature.
notes: Treats the star as a perfect blackbody sphere; real stars deviate from this. The temperature is the effective surface temperature in kelvin, and its fourth-power dependence makes the result very sensitive to it.

name: Absolute Magnitude from Luminosity
description: Converts a luminosity into an absolute magnitude relative to a zero-point luminosity, using -2.5 times the base-10 logarithm of their ratio. A brighter object yields a more negative (smaller) magnitude.
notes: The log is base 10, and the magnitude scale is inverted, so lower numbers are brighter. The result depends entirely on the chosen zero-point luminosity, which sets the reference.

name: Radiant Flux
description: Computes the radiant flux, or power per unit area, received at a distance from a source by spreading its luminosity over a sphere of radius d. Flux falls off as the inverse square of distance.
notes: Assumes the source radiates uniformly in all directions and no light is absorbed along the way. Distance is measured from the source center; doubling it quarters the flux.

name: Inverse-Square Brightness
description: Scales a known reference brightness to a new distance using the inverse-square law, multiplying by the square of the distance ratio (d0/d)². Moving farther away lowers the brightness.
notes: Both distances must use the same unit since only their ratio matters. It assumes no absorption or scattering between source and observer.

name: Wien's Peak Wavelength
description: Uses Wien's displacement law to find the wavelength at which a blackbody emits most strongly, dividing Wien's constant by the temperature. Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.
notes: Applies to an ideal blackbody, with temperature in kelvin. The peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature, so it shifts toward the blue as the object heats up.

name: Effective Temperature
description: Inverts the Stefan-Boltzmann law to recover a star's effective surface temperature from its luminosity and radius, taking the fourth root of L/(4πR²σ). It is the blackbody temperature matching the observed output.
notes: Gives the effective temperature of an equivalent blackbody, not a literal surface reading. Requires the radius and luminosity in consistent SI units, returning kelvin.

name: Synodic Period
description: Computes the synodic period, the time between successive alignments of two bodies, from their individual orbital periods as 1/(1/P1 - 1/P2). It is the apparent period seen from the faster body.
notes: The inner (faster) body should have the shorter period P1 so the result is positive. All periods share the same time unit, and the two periods must differ.

name: Kepler Semi-Major Axis
description: Solves Kepler's third law for the orbital semi-major axis, taking the cube root of GMP²/(4π²) from the central mass and orbital period. Longer periods correspond to larger orbits.
notes: Assumes the orbiting body's mass is negligible next to the central mass M. All inputs are in SI units, with the period in seconds, giving the axis in meters.

name: Parallax Distance (Parsec)
description: Converts a stellar parallax angle into distance in parsecs by taking its reciprocal. A parallax of one arcsecond corresponds to exactly one parsec.
notes: The parallax must be given in arcseconds for the result to come out in parsecs. Smaller, harder-to-measure angles mean larger distances, so measurement error grows with distance.

name: Redshift
description: Computes the dimensionless redshift z from the fractional shift of a spectral line, (observed minus emitted) divided by emitted wavelength. Positive values mean the source is receding.
notes: Both wavelengths must use the same unit; the result is unitless. A negative value indicates blueshift, and this simple form is not the relativistic Doppler formula at high speeds.

name: Recessional Velocity
description: Estimates the recessional velocity of a source by multiplying its redshift by the speed of light. This low-redshift approximation gives how fast the object moves away.
notes: Valid only for small redshifts (z much less than 1); at high z the relativistic formula is required and this overestimates the speed. The result is in the same units as the speed of light input.

name: Orbital Mass from Kepler
description: Derives the central mass from an orbit using Kepler's third law, 4π²a³/(GP²), from the semi-major axis and orbital period. It infers how much mass keeps a body on its measured orbit.
notes: Assumes the orbiting body's mass is negligible compared to the central mass; otherwise it gives the combined mass. All inputs must be in SI units, with the period in seconds.

name: Apparent Magnitude (Distance Modulus)
description: Applies the distance modulus, apparent equals absolute magnitude plus 5 log(d/10), to find how bright a star of known absolute magnitude appears at distance d. Farther stars appear fainter.
notes: Distance must be in parsecs, and the log is base 10. This ignores interstellar extinction, which would make the star appear fainter than the formula predicts.

name: Hubble Distance
description: Computes the Hubble distance c/H0, the scale at which the cosmological recession velocity would formally equal the speed of light. In meters it sets the characteristic size of the observable universe for a given Hubble constant.
notes: H0 must be in inverse seconds (SI), not the common km/s/Mpc form; convert first. The result is a characteristic scale, not a hard edge to the universe.

name: Hubble Time
description: Gives the Hubble time 1/H0, the inverse of the Hubble constant, in seconds. It provides a rough estimate of the age of the universe under simple expansion assumptions.
notes: H0 must be in SI inverse seconds. The Hubble time equals the true age only for particular expansion histories; the actual age depends on the matter and dark-energy content.

name: Critical Density of the Universe
description: Computes the critical density 3*H0^2/(8*pi*G) at which the universe's geometry is spatially flat. In kg/m^3 it is the total density that exactly balances expansion, and observed densities are compared to it as the density parameter Omega.
notes: H0 must be in SI inverse seconds. The value is extremely small (about 1e-26 kg/m^3); densities above it imply positive curvature and below it negative curvature.

name: Redshift from Scale Factor
description: Converts a cosmic scale factor a into the redshift z = 1/a - 1 of light emitted at that epoch. A smaller scale factor (earlier, more compressed universe) yields a larger redshift.
notes: Uses the convention that the present-day scale factor equals 1, so a must lie between 0 and 1 for a positive redshift. The dimensionless result is z.

name: Cosmic Scale Factor from Redshift
description: Gives the cosmic scale factor a = 1/(1 + z) at the epoch corresponding to a measured redshift z. It tells how much smaller the universe was, relative to today, when the observed light was emitted.
notes: Uses the convention that the present scale factor is 1, so the dimensionless result lies between 0 and 1 for positive z. It is the inverse of the redshift-from-scale-factor relation.

name: Cosmological Redshift (Wavelength)
description: Computes the observed wavelength lambda_e*(1 + z) of light that left a source with emitted wavelength lambda_e and traveled through an expanding universe of redshift z. The expansion stretches every wavelength by the factor (1 + z).
notes: Emitted wavelength and result share the same unit (meters). The stretch is due to cosmic expansion, distinct from a Doppler shift; z is the dimensionless redshift.

name: Density Parameter (Omega)
description: Gives the density parameter Omega = 8*pi*G*rho/(3*H0^2), the ratio of a component's mean density rho to the critical density. Omega equal to 1 means a flat universe, above 1 closed, and below 1 open.
notes: H0 must be in SI inverse seconds and rho in kg/m^3. The dimensionless Omega equals rho divided by the critical density; sum the Omegas of all components for the total.

name: Deceleration Parameter
description: Computes the cosmological deceleration parameter q0 = Om/2 - OL from the matter and dark-energy density parameters. A negative value signals accelerating expansion, as observed in the dark-energy-dominated universe.
notes: A flat two-component (matter plus cosmological-constant) model; here dark energy enters with equation of state w = -1. Negative q0 means the expansion is accelerating.

name: Friedmann Equation (Hubble Parameter)
description: Evaluates the Hubble parameter at redshift z, as H0*sqrt(Om*(1+z)^3 + Ok*(1+z)^2 + OL). Each term captures how matter, curvature, and dark energy dilute differently as the universe expands, giving the expansion rate at that epoch.
notes: Density parameters are today's values and should satisfy Om + Ok + OL = 1; result is in the same units as H0 (SI inverse seconds). Assumes dark energy with w = -1.

name: Matter-Radiation Equality Redshift
description: Gives the redshift Om/Or - 1 at which the matter and radiation densities of the universe were equal. Before this epoch radiation dominated the dynamics; afterward matter took over, shaping structure growth.
notes: Om and Or are the present-day matter and radiation density parameters. Because radiation dilutes faster (as (1+z)^4 versus (1+z)^3), equality occurs at high redshift, around a few thousand.

name: Comoving Distance (Low-z Approximation)
description: Estimates the comoving distance to an object at low redshift, as (c/H0)*z*(1 - z*(1+q0)/2). The leading term is Hubble's linear law, and the deceleration parameter q0 supplies the first correction.
notes: A Taylor expansion valid only for small z (roughly z < 0.3); it becomes inaccurate at high redshift. H0 must be in SI inverse seconds; result is in meters.

name: Luminosity Distance (Low-z Approximation)
description: Estimates the luminosity distance to a source at low redshift, as (c*z/H0)*(1 + (1-q0)*z/2). This distance sets how flux dims with distance, and the deceleration parameter q0 gives the first correction beyond Hubble's law.
notes: A low-redshift expansion (roughly z < 0.3) that fails at high z. Luminosity distance exceeds the comoving distance because of expansion; H0 in SI inverse seconds, result in meters.

name: Angular Diameter Distance
description: Converts the luminosity distance to the angular diameter distance via DL/(1 + z)^2. This distance relates an object's physical size to its apparent angular size, and unusually it can decrease at very high redshift.
notes: Uses the Etherington reciprocity relation linking the two distances by a factor (1+z)^2. DL is the luminosity distance and z the redshift; result is in the same length unit as DL.

name: Angular Size of Standard Ruler
description: Computes the angular size s/DA subtended by an object of physical size s at angular diameter distance DA, in radians. It applies the small-angle relation, valid when the object is much smaller than its distance.
notes: A small-angle approximation (angle roughly equals size over distance) requiring s much smaller than DA. Result is in radians; multiply by 206265 for arcseconds. Distances must use the angular diameter distance.

name: Jeans Length
description: Computes the Jeans length, the minimum size above which a gas cloud's self-gravity overcomes its thermal pressure and it collapses. In meters it grows with temperature and shrinks with density, marking the threshold for gravitational instability.
notes: Uses mean molecular weight mu times hydrogen mass mH for the particle mass; the numerical prefactor depends on the exact definition adopted. Warmer or thinner gas has a larger Jeans length.

name: Jeans Mass (Sphere Form)
description: Gives the Jeans mass as the gas contained in a sphere whose diameter equals the Jeans length, as (4/3)*pi*rho*(lam/2)^3. It represents the minimum mass that can gravitationally collapse at a given density.
notes: Here lam is the Jeans length and the radius is taken as lam/2; the numerical value depends on which fraction of the Jeans length is used as the radius. Result is in kg for SI inputs.

name: Jeans Mass (Thermal Form)
description: Computes the Jeans mass directly from thermodynamic quantities, as (5*kB*T/(G*mu*mH))^1.5 * (3/(4*pi*rho))^0.5. It gives the critical mass for gravitational collapse, rising with temperature and falling with density.
notes: The particle mass is mu times hydrogen mass mH; the leading constant depends on the exact Jeans-mass definition. Hotter or lower-density clouds require more mass to collapse.

name: CMB Temperature at Redshift z
description: Gives the temperature of the cosmic microwave background at redshift z, as T0*(1 + z). Because expansion cools the radiation in proportion to (1 + z), the CMB was hotter in the past, reaching thousands of kelvin near recombination.
notes: T0 is the present-day CMB temperature (about 2.725 K); result is in kelvin. The linear (1+z) scaling follows from adiabatic cosmic expansion of blackbody radiation.

name: CMB Blackbody Peak Frequency
description: Computes the frequency at which a blackbody spectrum at temperature T peaks in intensity per unit frequency, as 2.821*kB*T/h. Applied to the CMB it locates the microwave peak of the cosmic background spectrum.
notes: The constant 2.821 is Wien's displacement value for the frequency spectrum; the peak in wavelength gives a different location. Result is in hertz; T is the blackbody temperature.

name: CMB Photon Number Density
description: Gives the number of blackbody photons per cubic meter at temperature T, as (2*1.202/pi^2)*(kB*T/(hbar*c))^3. For the CMB it yields roughly 4e8 photons per cubic meter, one of the most abundant particle species in the universe.
notes: The factor 1.202 is the Riemann zeta function value zeta(3). Number density scales as T^3; T is the blackbody (CMB) temperature and the result is in photons per cubic meter.

name: Radiation Energy Density (Blackbody)
description: Computes the energy stored per unit volume in blackbody radiation at temperature T, as arad*T^4. This Stefan-Boltzmann relation shows the energy density rising steeply with the fourth power of temperature.
notes: arad is the radiation constant (4*sigma/c), distinct from the Stefan-Boltzmann constant sigma for surface flux. Result is in J/m^3; energy density scales as T^4.

name: Radiation Density Parameter
description: Computes the density parameter of radiation, the ratio of the present energy density of blackbody radiation (arad times T to the fourth) to the critical energy density (rhoc times c squared). It gives radiation as a dimensionless fraction of the total density that closes a flat universe.
notes: T should be the CMB temperature (about 2.725 K), giving a tiny value near 5e-5. This counts photons only; adding neutrinos raises the effective radiation density by roughly 1.68 times.

name: Photon-Baryon Sound Speed
description: Calculates the sound speed in the tightly coupled photon-baryon plasma of the early universe, c divided by the square root of 3 times (1 + R). R is the baryon-to-photon momentum density ratio, which lowers the speed below the pure-radiation value c/sqrt(3).
notes: R grows with the baryon density and decreasing redshift, so the sound speed drops over time. When R is zero the result reduces to c/sqrt(3), about 0.577c.

name: Gravitational Free-Fall Time
description: Gives the free-fall (collapse) timescale of a uniform, pressureless cloud of density rho under its own gravity, sqrt(3*pi/(32*G*rho)). It is the time for such a sphere to collapse to a point if only gravity acts.
notes: Depends only on density, not size or mass. Assumes no pressure support, rotation, or magnetic fields; real collapse is slowed by these. Denser regions collapse faster.

name: Dynamical Timescale
description: Computes the dynamical (orbital) timescale of a self-gravitating system, sqrt(r^3/(G*M)), for radius r enclosing mass M. It characterizes the time for material to orbit or cross the system and is close to the Keplerian orbital period divided by 2*pi.
notes: M is the mass enclosed within radius r. This is the free-fall or crossing time up to order-unity factors; multiply by 2*pi for the full circular orbital period.

name: Virial Mass
description: Estimates the mass of a gravitationally bound system from the virial theorem, 5*r*sigma^2/G, using the system radius r and the one-dimensional velocity dispersion sigma. It infers total mass, including dark matter, from the motions of its members.
notes: Assumes virial equilibrium and an isotropic velocity distribution; the numerical factor depends on the density profile. sigma is the line-of-sight (1D) dispersion, not the full 3D speed.

name: Virial Temperature
description: Gives the virial temperature of gas in a halo of mass M and radius r, G*M*mu*mH/(2*kB*r), the temperature at which the thermal energy of the gas balances its gravitational binding. It marks the typical temperature to which infalling gas is shock-heated.
notes: mu is the mean molecular weight (about 0.6 for ionized primordial gas); mu*mH is the mean particle mass. The order-unity prefactor varies with definition and profile.

name: Matter Density Evolution with Redshift
description: Computes how the mean matter density of the universe scales with redshift, rhom0*(1 + z)^3, from its present value rhom0. The cube reflects the dilution of matter as comoving volume expands by (1 + z)^3.
notes: z is dimensionless redshift; z = 0 recovers the present density. Applies to non-relativistic (dust) matter whose particle number is conserved as the universe expands.

name: Radiation Density Evolution with Redshift
description: Computes how the radiation energy density scales with redshift, rhor0*(1 + z)^4, from its present value rhor0. The fourth power combines the (1 + z)^3 volume dilution with an extra (1 + z) from the redshifting of photon energy.
notes: The extra factor of (1 + z) beyond matter comes from cosmological redshift lowering each photon's energy. Radiation therefore dominated at high z, before matter-radiation equality.

name: Dark Energy Density Evolution
description: Computes how dark energy density scales with redshift, rhod0*(1 + z)^(3*(1 + w)), for equation-of-state parameter w. For a cosmological constant (w = -1) the exponent is zero and the density stays constant; other w values make it evolve.
notes: w = -1 gives a constant density (the cosmological constant). w < -1 (phantom energy) makes density grow with time, while w > -1 makes it dilute as the universe expands.

name: Age of Universe (Einstein-de Sitter)
description: Gives the age of a flat, matter-only (Einstein-de Sitter) universe, 2/(3*H0), where H0 is the Hubble constant. It is two-thirds of the Hubble time 1/H0 for this simple matter-dominated model.
notes: H0 must be in inverse seconds (SI), not km/s/Mpc. This model ignores dark energy and so underestimates the real age; use the LCDM formula for an accurate value.

name: Age of Universe (Flat LCDM)
description: Computes the age of a flat LCDM universe with matter and a cosmological constant, using H0 and the density parameters OL (dark energy) and Om (matter). The closed-form expression integrates the expansion history to give the present cosmic age.
notes: Requires a flat universe with OL + Om = 1 and H0 in inverse seconds. The formula assumes w = -1 dark energy and neglects radiation, valid for the late-time universe.

name: Eddington Luminosity
description: Computes the Eddington luminosity, 4*pi*G*M*mp*c/sigmaT, the maximum luminosity at which radiation pressure on ionized hydrogen balances gravity for an accretor of mass M. Above it, outward radiation force overcomes inward gravity and halts steady accretion.
notes: Assumes spherical accretion of fully ionized hydrogen; mp and the Thomson cross section sigmaT set the electron scattering opacity. It scales linearly with mass, about 1.26e31 W per solar mass.

name: Eddington Accretion Rate
description: Computes the mass accretion rate needed to produce luminosity L at radiative efficiency eta, L/(eta*c^2). It inverts the relation L = eta*mdot*c^2, giving the rest-mass inflow whose fraction eta is radiated away.
notes: eta is the fraction of rest-mass energy converted to light (about 0.1 for a standard disk). Using the Eddington luminosity for L gives the Eddington accretion rate.

name: Chandrasekhar Mass Limit
description: Gives the Chandrasekhar mass, 5.83*Msun/mue^2, the maximum mass a white dwarf can have before electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support it against gravity. mue is the mean molecular weight per electron of the star's composition.
notes: For carbon-oxygen white dwarfs mue is about 2, giving roughly 1.46 solar masses. The numerical constant follows from the degenerate-electron equation of state.

name: Bondi Accretion Rate
description: Computes the spherically symmetric (Bondi) accretion rate onto a mass M from a uniform gas of density rho and sound speed cs, 4*pi*lam*(G*M)^2*rho/cs^3. It gives the steady inflow rate of gas gravitationally captured by the accretor.
notes: lam is a dimensionless eigenvalue set by the gas adiabatic index (about 0.25 for gamma = 5/3). Assumes steady, spherical, non-rotating accretion with negligible gas self-gravity.

name: Sunyaev-Zeldovich y-Parameter
description: Computes the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich Compton y-parameter, kB*Te/(me*c^2)*sigmaT*ne*L, measuring the distortion of the CMB spectrum as its photons scatter off hot electrons of temperature Te, density ne, along a path length L.
notes: It is the electron pressure integrated along the line of sight in units of me*c^2, times the Thomson optical depth. Typical galaxy-cluster values are around 1e-4, small but detectable.

name: Saha Ionization Equation
description: Evaluates the Saha ionization ratio, 2/ne*(2*pi*me*kB*T/h^2)^1.5*exp(-chi/(kB*T)), the ratio of ionized to neutral atom populations in thermal equilibrium at temperature T and electron density ne, for ionization energy chi.
notes: This is the two-level form with unit partition-function ratio; the Boltzmann factor uses ionization energy chi in joules. Valid in local thermodynamic equilibrium, as in stellar atmospheres.

name: Planck Mass
description: Computes the Planck mass, sqrt(hbar*c/G), the fundamental mass scale formed from the reduced Planck constant, the speed of light, and the gravitational constant. It marks the scale where quantum and gravitational effects become comparable.
notes: Uses the reduced Planck constant hbar. The result is about 2.18e-8 kg, macroscopic yet the natural mass unit of quantum gravity. Some define it with h instead of hbar.

name: Planck Time
description: Computes the Planck time, sqrt(hbar*G/c^5), the fundamental time scale built from the reduced Planck constant, gravitational constant, and speed of light. It is the shortest time interval that has operational meaning in known physics.
notes: Uses the reduced Planck constant hbar. The value is about 5.4e-44 s. It equals the Planck length divided by the speed of light.

name: Planck Temperature
description: Computes the Planck temperature, sqrt(hbar*c^5/G)/kB, the fundamental temperature scale set by dividing the Planck energy by the Boltzmann constant. It represents the temperature scale at which quantum gravity is expected to dominate.
notes: Uses the reduced Planck constant hbar. The value is about 1.4e32 K. It is the Planck energy expressed as a temperature via E = kB*T.

name: Planck Energy
description: Computes the Planck energy, sqrt(hbar*c^5/G), the fundamental energy scale formed from the reduced Planck constant, speed of light, and gravitational constant. It sets the energy at which quantum gravitational effects are expected to become important.
notes: Uses the reduced Planck constant hbar. The value is about 1.96e9 J, or roughly 1.22e19 GeV, enormous for a single quantum. It equals the Planck mass times c squared.

name: de Sitter Horizon Radius
description: Computes the de Sitter horizon radius, sqrt(3/Lam), the characteristic size of the cosmological event horizon in a universe dominated by a positive cosmological constant Lam. It sets the maximum distance from which signals can ever reach an observer.
notes: Lam here has units of inverse length squared (a curvature). The radius grows as Lam shrinks; the observed small Lam gives a horizon of order the present Hubble radius.

name: Cosmological Constant from Vacuum Density
description: Computes the cosmological constant Lambda from a vacuum energy density rhov, 8*pi*G*rhov/c^2. It converts a mass-equivalent vacuum density into the curvature-scale Lambda that appears in Einstein's field equations.
notes: rhov is a mass density (kg/m^3); the c^2 converts it to an energy density. The result has units of inverse length squared. This links dark energy density to the geometric Lambda.

name: Combined Magnitude of Two Stars
description: Gives the total magnitude of two unresolved stars by adding their fluxes, not their magnitudes.
notes: Two equal stars appear 0.753 magnitudes brighter than one.

name: Star Temperature from B−V Colour (Ballesteros)
description: Estimates a star's effective temperature from its B−V colour, treating it as a blackbody (Ballesteros 2012).
notes: The Sun (B−V ≈ 0.65) gives about 5780 K.

name: Mass–Luminosity Relation
description: Estimates a main-sequence star's luminosity from its mass: L ∝ M^3.5 for roughly Sun-like masses.
notes: Twice the Sun's mass shines about 11 times as bright.

name: Main-Sequence Lifetime
description: Estimates how long a star stays on the main sequence: fuel ∝ M, burn rate ∝ M^3.5, so life ∝ M^−2.5 (Sun ≈ 10 billion years).
notes: Massive stars live only millions of years.

name: Stellar Radius from Luminosity and Temperature
description: Gives a star's radius in solar radii from the Stefan–Boltzmann law L = 4πR²σT⁴.
notes: Cool but luminous stars must be giants.

name: Cepheid Absolute Magnitude from Period
description: Gives the absolute visual magnitude of a classical Cepheid from its period (Leavitt law, Benedict et al. 2007) — a cosmic distance ladder rung.
notes: Compare with the apparent magnitude for the distance.

name: Tangential Velocity from Proper Motion
description: Converts a star's proper motion and distance into its speed across the line of sight.
notes: Combine with radial velocity for the space velocity.

name: Solar Irradiance at a Planet
description: Gives the sunlight intensity above the atmosphere at a distance from the Sun (inverse-square law).
notes: Mars receives about 586 W/m², 43 % of Earth's.

name: Accretion Luminosity
description: Gives the power released as matter falls onto a compact object from far away.
notes: Onto a neutron star this turns roughly 10–20 % of the rest mass into radiation.

name: Moon Illuminated Fraction
description: Gives the fraction of the Moon's disc that is lit from the angle between Sun and Moon as seen from Earth.
notes: 90° is first quarter (half lit); 180° full moon.

name: Transit Depth
description: Gives the fractional dip in a star's brightness when a planet passes in front of it.
notes: Jupiter across the Sun: about 1 %; Earth: about 0.0084 %.

name: Planet Equilibrium Temperature
description: Gives a planet's temperature if it absorbed starlight and radiated as a blackbody, ignoring greenhouse warming.
notes: Earth comes out at about 255 K; the greenhouse effect adds about 33 K.

name: Habitable Zone Distance
description: Gives the distance at which a planet receives a given stellar flux; about 1.1 S⊕ marks the inner edge and 0.36 S⊕ the outer edge (Kopparapu et al. 2013).
notes: For the Sun the conservative zone spans about 0.95–1.67 AU.

name: Radial Velocity Semi-Amplitude
expression: (2 * pi * g_newton / p)^(1 / 3) * mp * sin(rad(inc)) / ms^(2 / 3)
description: Gives how fast a star wobbles towards and away from us because of an orbiting planet (circular orbit, planet much lighter than the star).
notes: Jupiter makes the Sun move about 12.5 m/s at its own period; here it is placed at 1 year.

name: Transit Duration (Central Transit)
description: Gives the approximate length of a central transit for a planet much smaller than its star.
notes: An Earth analogue transits a Sun-like star for about 13 hours.

name: Telescope Limiting Magnitude
description: Estimates the faintest star visible through a telescope of a given aperture under dark skies.
notes: An 8-inch (200 mm) telescope reaches about magnitude 13.5.

name: Dawes Resolution Limit
description: Gives the closest separation of two equal stars a telescope can just split (Dawes 1867).
notes: Seeing usually limits large telescopes to about 1 arcsecond.

name: Exit Pupil
description: Gives the width of the beam leaving the eyepiece; about 5–7 mm matches a dark-adapted eye.
notes: Larger than the eye's pupil wastes light.

name: True Field of View
description: Gives the actual sky area seen through an eyepiece.
notes: The full Moon is about 0.5° across.

name: Image Pixel Scale
description: Gives the sky angle covered by one camera pixel on a telescope.
notes: Match about 1/2–1/3 of the seeing for good sampling.

name: Atmospheric Extinction Correction
description: Corrects a measured magnitude to what it would be above the atmosphere.
notes: k is about 0.2 in V at a good site, larger in blue light.
